newsitem.title: USA: Auditors appointed to hunt Swiss Holocaust money.
newsitem.headline: Auditors appointed to hunt Swiss Holocaust money.

text.p: The commission probing whether Swiss banks hold the unclaimed wealth of Holocaust victims on Tuesday named half of the world's "Big Six" accounting firms to help while its chairman denied that the probe would also extend to tracing assets looted by the Nazis.

Former U.S. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Paul Volcker, head of the "Independent Committee of Eminent Persons," said the group had chosen accounting firms Arthur Andersen, KPMG Peat Marwick and Price Waterhouse to conduct "investigative audits" of Swiss banks.
Volcker told a news conference here a preliminary search would start as early as next week and said he hoped an entire audit of 450 Swiss banks would be completed by mid-1998.

Volcker insisted that the commission, which has three members appointed by Jewish groups and three by the Swiss Bankers Association, was only trying to determine whether the dormant accounts were from Jews and others fearing persecution by the Nazis before and during the Second World War.

"Our mandate does not extend to looted money, gold or other assets," Volcker said, adding that any information the commission turned up in its investigation on looted wealth would be turned over to a separate Swiss probe for action.

A memorandum released by Volcker at the press conference said the auditors were instructed to report to the committee any evidence they turned up on "accounts containing looted assets or information indicating a breach of fiduciary duty ... so that the (committee) can take appropriate action ... to report this information to the Swiss government."

Volcker said it was also not the committee's job to return dormant accounts to Holocaust survivors or their relatives -- that was the task of the Swiss Banking ombdusman whose own work has come under fire from Jewish groups.

"Our job is not to sit in judgment on the ombudsman. ... Our job is to draw a line and say this is all we can know about these dormant accounts," Volcker said, adding that the Swiss banks are giving the auditors unprecedented access to their accounts.

The committee was formed in May by the World Jewish Congress and Swiss bankers after accusations that Swiss banks profited cynically from the Holocaust and then stonewalled relatives trying to find family members' wealth. Swiss banks denied the charges, but agreed to the probe.

The Swiss Bankers Association (SBA) said early this year that banks had discovered 38.7 million Swiss francs ($30.5 million) in accounts opened by customers before the end of the war and dormant since at least 1985. Since then some banks have identified additional accounts which could increase the total amount of such dormant accounts by 10 percent.
Not all these funds were necessarily owned by Jews killed in the Holocaust, Swiss bankers said.

The Swiss government had ordered banks in 1962 to conduct a similar sweep for dormant accounts of Nazi victims. The sweep turned up 9.5 million francs ($7.5 million), of which 75 percent was returned to heirs and the rest given to the Swiss Jewish community and a group that helps refugees.

Volcker said that in first phase of the new search, audit companies will gather data and establish the framework they need to go about their work. They will test it in pilot audits of a representative sampling of Swiss banks.
Based on this experience, a full-scale audit programme will start in about six months as the firms pore over banks' books with full access to their records.
Volcker said more accounting firms could be added to the search when the full-scale hunt begins and that all would be paid at internationally acceptable hourly rates.
